The Right Wing (Rajput) of the 5th Light Infantry (Indian Army) revolted against British rule on 15 February 1915, killing more than 40 British officers and residents as well as local civilians. The mutiny continued for ten days before being suppressed with the support of the Singapore Volunteer Artillery, additional British troopers, military men despatched by the Sultan of Johor and men from the Allied forces including Japan. A Court of Inquiry was held on 23 February 1915 and concluded by 15 May, leading to 36 mutineers being executed, 77 officers transported and 12 imprisoned.

Riot. Economic event. The crisis started in Thailand on 2 July 1997, in which there was a sharp depreciation of the Thai baht against the US dollar. Some Asian countries, such as Indonesia, also experienced sharp declines in the values of their currencies, which disrupted their economies. Singapore was not directly hit but was affected by the regional economic slowdown and fell into recession in the second half of 1998. Regional economies started to recover in 1999.

The Battle of Opium Hill, which took place on 14 February 1942 at Pasir Panjang, was one of the fiercest battles Singapore experienced against an invading Japanese army during World War II. The outnumbered troops of the 1st Malay Brigade of the Malay Regiment, led by Lieutenant Adnan Saidi, valiantly fought the Japanese to the death.

The Battle of Singapore took place from 8 to 15 February 1942 between the Allied (mainly British Commonwealth) and Japanese armies. On 8 February 1942, the first Japanese troops landed in Singapore on Singapore's northwestern coastline. The British surrendered Singapore to the Japanese forces after a week of intense fighting.

The British announced on 18 July 1967 its plan to withdraw its forces from Singapore by the mid-1970s. However, the deadline was brought forward to 1971. The sudden pullout of British troops posed serious problems to Singapore's defense and economy. To overcome the crisis, Singapore embarked on a rapid industralisation programme and new labour laws were passed to attract foreign investments. Singapore also tightened its defenses through military cooperation with other countries and tripled its military spending.

The Chinese Post Office Riots of 15 December 1876 refer to a fierce protest by the local Chinese against the establishment of government-regulated post office to collect all China-bound letters and remittances. The Kempeitai raided the cells in Changi Prison on 10 October 1943, interrogating and torturing the prisoners, resulting in 15 deaths.

Epidemic. Between February and May 2003, there was an outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) in Singapore. Part of a global epidemic, the SARS virus infected 238 people in Singapore, mostly health-care workers and their family members, killing 33 of them. The infected were treated at Tan Tock Seng Hospital and the Communicable Diseases Centre. Government measures like the closure of schools, home quarantines and thorough screening of visitors to Singapore helped to contain the epidemic by May 2003.

Accident. SilkAir flight MI 185 (flying from Jakarta to Singapore) crashed into the Musi River near Palembang in South Sumatra, Indonesia on 19 December 1997 at about 4.13 pm local time, killing all 104 people on board. A search and rescue mission was conducted but soon became a search and recovery operation which ended in mid-January 1988 after most parts of the plane, including the black box, were recovered. Official investigations were led by the National Transportation Safety Committee of Indonesia and assisted by the National Transportation Safety Board of the United States, the Singapore Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Australian Bureau of Air Safety Investigation. The final report was released on 14 December 2000.

The inaugural Youth Olympic Games, hosted by Singapore from 14 to 26 August 2010, for 14–18-year-olds competing in 26 sports. The event drew an estimated 3,600 athletes from 205 countries, attracted about 370,000 spectators and involved some 20,000 local and international volunteers. Singapore competed against 11 other cities to host the Games, eventually trumping rival candidate Moscow by 53 to 44 votes to host it. Singapore finished the Games with six medals – two silver medals for swimming and table-tennis, two bronze medals for taekwondo, and one bronze medal each for archery, sailing and football.

Singapore Airlines Flight SQ006 (flying from Singapore to Los Angeles via Taiwan) crashed on a closed runway at Chiang Kai-shek Airport during takeoff on 31 October 2000 at 11.18 pm local time, destroying the Boeing 747-400 aircraft and killing 83 of the 179 people on board. Initial on-scene investigation was conducted by representatives from Singapore, the United States and Taiwan. Taiwan's Aviation Safety Council (ASC) released reports of the incident on 23 February 2001 and 26 April 2002, and Singapore's Ministry of Transport released its own report on 26 April 2002.

Accident. Singapore Airlines Flight 117 (a shuttle service from Kuala Lumpur to Singapore) was hijacked on 26 March 1991 at 10.15 pm. Four passengers claiming to be members of the Pakistan People's Party took control of the plane and issued a list of demands, including the release of nine prisoners detained in Pakistan. The crisis ended on 27 March1991 at Changi International Airport when a team of Singapore Armed Forces commandos conducted a rescue operation that killed the hijackers.

On 7 June 1947, the government set 23 August to 27 September 1947 as the dates for the first post-war pan-Malayan census to be taken. M. V. del Tufo was officially appointed Superintendent of Census, who faced a lot of challenges when conducting the 1947 census. There were fears that this census was similar to the Japanese Occupation household data collection, and others were afraid to supply personal information. Measures were taken to reassure the public in order for the census to collect accurate data from the population.

The Singapore Glass Manufacturers Co. Ltd. (popularly known as the Singapore Glass Factory) was the only manufacturer of glass containers in Singapore. The factory, with more than 1,000 workers, provided much needed employment to the residents. However, relations between the Company and its employees had been strained due to several issues, this had resulted a strike on 28 August 1960. The strike lasted for 73 days before the dispute was resolved, and staff returned to work on 9 November.

Political event. A Japanese military operation named Sook Ching operation was carried out from 21 February to 4 March 1942. Chinese males between the ages of 18 and 50 were summoned to various mass screening centres and those suspected of being anti-Japanese were executed. Massacre sites include Changi, Punggol and Bedok. In 1947, seven Japanese officers were charged during a war crimes trial in Singapore for their participation in Operation Sook Ching.

Campaign. Started on 7 September 1979 by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew. The aim of the campaign was to encourage the speaking of Mandarin among Chinese Singaporeans of various dialect groups and also to support the government's bilingual policies. Activities include conducting Mandarin classes for Chinese civil servants and members of public. Mandarin lessons were also made available over the phone for members of public.

Accident. Greek tanker, S. T. Spyros, owned by Ulysses Tanker Corporation of Liberia and operated by International Operations, S A, exploded in flames at Jurong Shipyard on 12 October 1978 at 2.15 pm. The vessel was undergoing repairs at the shipyard when sparks from a cutting torch started a fire which left 76 dead and 69 injured. A Committee of Inquiry led by Senior District Judge, Michael Khoo Kah Lip was set up to investigate the cause of the fire.

Strike. The strike arose from a dispute over the terms of reinstatement of a dismissed worker on 3 February 1954. The Straits Times management dismissed the workers who took part in the walkout. The workers realised that their action was illegal and reported for work on 8 February, but they were locked out of the premises. Singapore Printing Employees' Union negotiated with the management and the workers voted to end the dispute and return to work on 22 February.

On 2 September 1945, the Japanese signed the Instrument of Surrender on board an American battleship, Missouri, in Tokyo Bay, officially ended the World War II. Another surrender ceremony was held at the Municipal Building of Singapore (now known as City Hall) on 12 September 1945, marked the ending of Japanese Occupation in Southeast Asia.

Percival, was ordered to be at Ford Factory. Yamashita demanded an unconditional surrender of Singapore. Percival on behalf of the British, signed the Singapore Surrender Document.

Campaign. The Tree Planting campaign was started by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in 1963 to plant a minimum of 10,000 saplings a year throughout Singapore. The aim of the campaign was to transform Singapore into a garden city. In 1971, the annual tree planting day was started with the participation of ministers and members of parliament. In 1992, it was launched as part of the Clean and Green Week campaign.

Economic event. The United States-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (USSFTA) was signed by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and President George W. Bush on 6 May 2003 in Washington DC. It was ratified by the US House of Representatives on 25 July 2003 and by the Senate on 1 August 2003. It was implemented on 1 January 2004. Besides the tariff concessions, the agreement also allowed easier movement of citizens from both countries.
